snapshot.title: UPSC History: Decline of Mughals & Regional Powers
snapshot.exam_hook: 🏔️ UPSC History Hook: 1707: Aurangzeb dies. 1739: Nadir Shah. Hyderabad: Nizam. Awadh: Saadat Khan. Bengal: Murshid Quli. Khalsa: Guru Gobind Singh.

quick_notes.title: Causes of Mughal Decline
quick_notes.detail: Weak successors. Jagirdari Crisis (shortage of land). Financial bankruptcy due to Aurangzeb's wars. Invasions : Nadir Shah (1739 - took Peacock Throne), Abdali (Panipat III). Rise of autonomous states.
quick_notes.explanation: The Mughal Empire declined because of weak successors, meaning later emperors after Aurangzeb lacked the skill and authority to control the vast empire. A major internal problem was the Jagirdari Crisis, where there was a shortage of land (jagirs) to give to nobles as payment, causing corruption and rebellion. The empire also faced financial bankruptcy, or complete lack of money, because Aurangzeb's long and expensive wars in the Deccan region drained the treasury. Foreign invasions weakened the empire further: in 1739, Nadir Shah of Persia invaded and took the famous Peacock Throne, and later Ahmad Shah Abdali of Afghanistan defeated the Mughals at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761. Finally, as central control collapsed, many autonomous states, or self-governing regions like Bengal and Hyderabad, broke away and became independent.

quick_notes.title: Successor States
quick_notes.detail: Hyderabad: Founded by Nizam-ul-Mulk (Asaf Jah) in 1724. Bengal : Murshid Quli Khan. Awadh : Saadat Khan (Burhan-ul-Mulk). These states nominally accepted Mughal authority but were independent.
quick_notes.explanation: Successor States were new kingdoms that formed when the Mughal Empire started to weaken in the 1700s. Hyderabad was one such state, founded in 1724 by Nizam-ul-Mulk, also known as Asaf Jah, who was a former Mughal governor. Bengal became a separate state under Murshid Quli Khan, who was also a Mughal governor who seized control. Awadh was founded by Saadat Khan, also called Burhan-ul-Mulk, another Mughal governor who established his own rule. These three states nominally accepted Mughal authority, meaning they pretended to be loyal to the Mughal emperor, but in reality they acted independently and made their own decisions.

quick_notes.title: The Sikhs
quick_notes.detail: Transformed into a military brotherhood by Guru Gobind Singh (Khalsa). Rise of Ranjit Singh (Sher-e-Punjab) who unified the Misls and established the Sikh Empire in Punjab.
quick_notes.explanation: TheSikhs began as a religious community, but Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, transformed them into a military brotherhood called the Khalsa, which means "pure" and refers to the community of initiated Sikhs who follow a strict code of conduct. Later, the Sikhs were organized into several independent warrior groups known as Misls. A leader named Ranjit Singh, also called Sher-e-Punjab meaning "Lion of Punjab," united these Misls and founded the Sikh Empire in the Punjab region of South Asia.

quick_notes.title: Mysore & Hyder Ali
quick_notes.detail: Rise of Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan in the South. They modernised the army and posed a serious challenge to the British.
quick_notes.explanation: Hyder Ali was a military leader who rose to power in the kingdom of Mysore, located in southern India, during the mid-1700s. He took control of Mysore by pushing aside the old Hindu ruler, and he is known for modernizing his army by training soldiers to use European-style weapons and tactics, including using rockets in warfare. His son, Tipu Sultan, continued this work and became the ruler after Hyder Ali died. Together, they fought several wars against the British East India Company, which was a British trading company that had become a powerful political and military force in India. The British East India Company, often simply called the Company, controlled large parts of India through its own army and was trying to expand its territory. Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan posed a serious challenge to the British because their modernized army was strong enough to win battles against the Company's forces, making them one of the most dangerous enemies the British faced in the south.

quick_notes.title: The Jats & Rajputs
quick_notes.detail: Jats: Suraj Mal (Plato of the Jats). Rajputs : Amber, Marwar regained independence but faced internal conflicts.
quick_notes.explanation: The Jats and Rajputs were two powerful groups in 18th-century India who built their own kingdoms after the Mughal Empire weakened. The Jats were a farming and warrior community, and their most famous leader was Suraj Mal, who is sometimes called the Plato of the Jats because he was a wise and just ruler. He built the strong fort of Bharatpur and created a well-organized state. The Rajputs were a warrior clan from Rajasthan, and two of their major kingdoms, Amber (also called Jaipur) and Marwar (also called Jodhpur), managed to win back their independence from the Mughals. However, after gaining freedom, these Rajput kingdoms fought among themselves in internal conflicts, which made them weaker. So, while both groups successfully broke away from Mughal control, the Rajputs were divided by their own fights, whereas the Jats under Suraj Mal built a more stable and united kingdom.

topic_title: UPSC History: Decline of Mughals & Regional Powers
lesson_intro: Today we study the 'Great Fragmentation'. After the death of Aurangzeb in 1707, the Mughal Empire rapidly declined, giving way to independent regional powers like Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad, and the Sikhs. We focus on the 'Later Mughals' (the 'Kings of Delhi') and the causes of decline—from the Jagirdari crisis to the invasions of Nadir Shah and Ahmad Shah Abdali. For UPSC, understanding how these regional states formed is the bridge to Modern History and the British conquest.
